      AtomStructure IStructure II
      B

  2. The structure of the ion was experimentall determine using x−-−ray diffraction:

      • all nine atoms lie on a plane
      • B−O(bridging)\ce{B-O(bridging)}B−O(bridging): 143.3 pm

      • B−O(terminal)\ce{B-O(terminal)}B−O(terminal): 128.0 pm

    1. State which structure is consistent with the planar geometry. Justify your answer with reference to the hybridization of the bridging oxygen atoms. [3]

    2. The B−O(bridging)\ce{B-O(bridging)}B−O(bridging) bonds are longer than B−O(terminal)\ce{B-O(terminal)}B−O(terminal) bonds but shorter than typical B−O\ce{B-O}B−O single bonds (148 pm). Explain this observation using the concept of bond order. [2]

    3. The benzene molecule (CX6HX6)(\ce{C6H6})(CX6​HX6​) also contains a planar six−-−membered ring. Explain why benzene has equal C−C\ce{C-C}C−C bond lengths while metaborate, BX3OX6X3−\ce{B3O6^{3-}}BX3​OX6​X3− has two different B−O\ce{B-O}B−O bond lengths. [2]

      Award M1 for correct formal charges on Structure I.

      Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
      Formal charge is calculated according to the equation

      FC=#valence electrons−#lone pair electrons−#bonds\textrm{FC} = \#\textrm{valence electrons} - \# \textrm{lone pair electrons} - \#\textrm{bonds}FC=#valence electrons−#lone pair electrons−#bonds

      In Structure I, consider boron first. Boron has three valence electrons, no lone pair electrons, and forms three bonds. It has a formal charge of 0. The bridging oxygen has six valence electrons, four lone pair electrons, and two bonds. It also has a formal charge of 0. The terminal oxygen has six valence electrons, six lone pair electrons and forms one bond. Its formal charge is −1.-1.−1. As a check, the sum of the formal charges must equal to the overall charge on the ion.

    2. Structure I ✓\checkmark✓
      minimize formal charge in the molecule
      OR
      most electronegative atom (O) has more negative formal charge ✓\checkmark✓

      Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
      When evaluating Lewis structures, negative formal change should be placed on the more electronegative oxygen atoms, and the preferred structure will minimize the number of nonzero formal charges. Both considerations favor Structure I where oxygen has a −1-1−1 formal change and there are fewer atoms with nonzero formal charge, indicating less charge separation.

    1. Structure II ✓\checkmark✓
      Structure I has sp3sp^3sp3 hybridized O atoms, tetrahedral geometry / nonplanar ✓\checkmark✓
      Structure II has sp2sp^2sp2 hybridized O atoms, trigonal planar geometry / planar ✓\checkmark✓

      Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
      Structure II is planar. Each boron and oxygen has three electron domains forming three σ−\sigma-σ−bonds arranged in a trigonal planar geometry. This requires sp2sp^2sp2 hybridization, which produces 120°120\degree120° bond angles and permits all atoms in the ring to lie in the same plane. The remaining unhybridized p−p-p− orbitals on boron and oxygen overlap to produce a delocalized π−\pi-π−system that stabilizes the planar structure.

      Structure I is nonplanar. The bridging oxygen atoms are sp3−sp^3-sp3−hybridized with four electron domains, giving a tetrahedral arrangement. This geometry does not place the B−O−B\ce{B-O-B}B−O−B linkages in the same plane.

    2. delocalized π−\pi-π−bonding between B and O atoms ✓\checkmark✓
      B−O\ce{B-O}B−O bond order greater than 1 ✓\checkmark✓

      Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
      Bond length is a powerful indirect measure of bond order: higher bond order (more shared electron density between two nuclei, especially involving π−\pi-π−bonding) leads to shorter, stronger bonds. This shorter B−O\ce{B-O}B−O bond indicates partial double−-−bond character, i.e. bond order > 1 but < 2. The natural explanation is that the π−\pi-π−electrons are delocalized across the entire BX3OX6X3−\ce{B3O6^{3-}}BX3​OX6​X3− framework.

    3. benzene: C atoms are equivalent; uniform π−\pi-π−electron density, identical C−C\ce{C-C}C−C bond orders and lengths ✓\checkmark✓
      metaborate: bridging and terminal O atoms are inequivalent; nonuniform π−\pi-π−electron density, two distinct B−O\ce{B-O}B−O bond orders and lengths ✓\checkmark✓

      Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
      In benzene, all six carbon atoms are identical, each participating equally in the delocalized π−\pi-π−system. Because the electron density is distributed uniformly around the ring, every C−C\ce{C-C}C−C bond acquires the same bond order (1.5) and all C−C\ce{C-C}C−C bonds are the same length.

      In metaborate ion, the oxygen atoms are in different environments. Terminal O atoms are bonded to only one boron atom and seem to have greater B=O\ce{B=O}B=O character. Bridging O atoms are bonded to two boron atoms and have less π−\pi-π−character. Because the two oxygen types are structurally and electronically distinct, the π−\pi-π−electron density is not distributed evenly. As a result there are two different B−O\ce{B-O}B−O bond orders and two different B−O\ce{B-O}B−O bond lengths.

  1. nickel ions distort the regular arrangement of zinc cations in the lattice
    OR
    nickel ions are smaller than zinc ions ✓\checkmark✓
    prevent layers sliding over each other ✓\checkmark✓

    Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
    In pure zinc, the metal cations are arranged in regular, identical layers. When a force is applied, these layers can slide easily over one another, so pure zinc is relatively soft.

    In the alloy, some zinc cations are replaced by nickel cations of a different size. This causes distortions in the metallic lattice, so the layers can no longer slide past each other easily. As a result, more force is required to move the layers, and the alloy is harder than pure zinc.

    1. Any three of the following:

      • d−-−orbitals are split (by the ligands) ✓\checkmark✓
      • light absorbed promotes d−d-d−electrons ✓\checkmark✓
      • energy gap corresponds to red light being absorbed ✓\checkmark✓
      • complementary color is observed ✓\checkmark✓

      Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
      In aqueous nickel(II) ions, the water ligands create an electric field around the metal ion, which splits the five d−d-d−orbitals into two energy levels.

      Electrons in the lower d−d-d−orbitals absorb visible light to move to the higher d−d-d−orbitals. The energy gap corresponds to a specific wavelength of light in the visible region. Red light is absorbed, and green, the complementary color, is observed.

    2. no d–dd\text{--}dd–d transition possible because d−d-d−orbitals are filled ✓\checkmark✓

      Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
      Zn(II) has a full ddd subshell, the electron configuration is 1s22s22p63s23p63d10.1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 3d^{10}.1s22s22p63s23p63d10. Because all d−d-d−orbitals are completely filled, there are no possible d–dd\textrm{--}dd–d transitions.

      Since no visible light is absorbed, the solution appears colorless.

    3. octahedral AND 90°\degree° and 180° ✓\degree \: \checkmark°✓

      Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
      With six identical ligands arranged around the metal ion, the structure is octahedral. In an octahedral geometry, the bond angles are 90°90\degree90° between adjacent ligands and 180°180\degree180° across the metal center.

    1. harder to remove an electron from an ion with increasing positive charge ✓\checkmark✓

      Further Explanation:‾\underline{\textrm{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
      Each time an electron is removed, the ion formed has a greater positive charge. The remaining electrons experience a stronger electrostatic attraction to the nucleus. Therefore, each successive ionization requires more energy than the previous one.

    2. IE values of Ni gradually increase AND Mg shows a sharp increase after IE2 ✓\textrm{IE}_2 \:\checkmarkIE2​✓
      Mg always loses two electrons ✓\checkmark✓
      further IEs of Ni are similar in energy, so oxidation state can vary ✓\checkmark✓

      Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
      For magnesium, the first two ionization energies increase gradually, but the third ionization energy is extremely large. This indicates removal of an electron from a new inner shell, which is energetically unfavorable. Therefore, Mg forms only +2 oxidation state.

      For nickel, successive ionization energies increase more gradually without a single massive jump. This means electrons are removed from orbitals of similar energy, so Ni can feasibly lose different numbers of electrons. As a result, nickel can form multiple oxidation states such as +2 and +3.

      The measured specific optical rotation of α=+13.52°\alpha =+13.52\degreeα=+13.52° shows that the product is optically active and therefore not racemic. In nucleophilic substitution at a chiral center:

        • SN_\textrm{N}N​1 reactions form planar carbocations, which are attacked from either side leading to a racemic product mixture and no specific optical rotation (α=0°).(\alpha = 0\degree).(α=0°).

        • SN_\textrm{N}N​2 reactions proceed by backside attack and inversion of the stereocenter, yielding a single enantiomer with a net specific optical rotation.

      Since the rotation is +13.52°,+13.52\degree,+13.52°, the product is not racemic, therefore the first step proceeds via SN_\textrm{N}N​2 and involves stereochemical inversion at the chiral carbon.

      This distinguishes SN_\textrm{N}N​2 from SN_\textrm{N}N​1, where the rate law depends only on the substrate.

    Electrode B (cathode): OX2+4 HX++4 eX−⟶2 HX2O ✓\ce{O2} + 4\ce{\,H+} + 4 \ce{\,e-} \longrightarrow 2 \ce{\,H2O} \: \checkmarkOX2​+4HX++4eX−⟶2HX2​O✓

    Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
    The fuel cell shows butan−-−2−-−ol being oxidized at the anode to produce carbon dioxide and electrons. The electrons flow to the cathode so that reduction occurs and oxygen gas is transformed to water.

    To balance the redox reaction consider each half reaction separately.

    CX4HX9OH⟶COX2\ce{C4H9OH} \longrightarrow \ce{CO2}CX4​HX9​OH⟶COX2​

    OX2⟶HX2O\ce{O2} \longrightarrow \ce{H2O}OX2​⟶HX2​O

    Balance everything but the hydrogen and oxygen:

    CX4HX9OH⟶4 COX2\ce{C4H9OH} \longrightarrow \ce{4\,CO2}CX4​HX9​OH⟶4COX2​

    OX2⟶HX2O\ce{O2} \longrightarrow \ce{H2O}OX2​⟶HX2​O

    Assign oxidation states and account for the electrons lost and gained. The oxidation state of carbon in carbon dioxide is +4, in butan−-−2−-−ol is −2-2−2. With four electrons losing 6 electrons the total electrons lost is 24. The oxidation state of oxygen in water is −2-2−2 and in oxygen gas is 0. Each oxygen gains 2 electrons so overall 4 electrons are gained.

    C−2X4HX9OH+7 HX2O⟶4 C+4OX2+24 eX−\ce{\overset{\textcolor{red}{-2}}{C}_4H9OH} + 7\ce{\,H2O} \longrightarrow \ce{4\,\overset{\textcolor{red}{+4}}{C}O2} + 24 \ce{\,e-}C−2X4​HX9​OH+7HX2​O⟶4C+4OX2​+24eX−

    O0X2+4 eX−⟶2 HX2O−2\ce{\overset{\textcolor{red}{0}}{O}_2} + 4\ce{\,e-} \longrightarrow \ce{2\,H2\overset{\textcolor{red}{-2}}{O}}O0X2​+4eX−⟶2HX2​O−2

    Balance the oxygen with with water:

    CX4HX9OH+7 HX2O⟶4 COX2+24 eX−\ce{C4H9OH} + 7\ce{\,H2O} \longrightarrow \ce{4\,CO2} + 24 \ce{\,e-}CX4​HX9​OH+7HX2​O⟶4COX2​+24eX−

    OX2+4 eX−⟶2 HX2O\ce{O2} + 4 \ce{\,e-} \longrightarrow \ce{2\,H2O}OX2​+4eX−⟶2HX2​O

    Balance the hydrogen with HX+:\ce{H+}:HX+:

    CX4HX9OH+7 HX2O⟶4 COX2+24 eX−+24 HX+\answer{\ce{C4H9OH} + 7\ce{\,H2O} \longrightarrow \ce{4\,CO2} + 24 \ce{\,e-} + 24 \ce{\,H+}}CX4​HX9​OH+7HX2​O⟶4COX2​+24eX−+24HX+​

    OX2+4 eX−+4 HX+⟶2 HX2O\answer{\ce{O2} + 4 \ce{\,e-} + 4 \ce{\,H+} \longrightarrow \ce{2\,H2O}}OX2​+4eX−+4HX+⟶2HX2​O​

    The sum of the two half reactions is the combustion of the fuel. To combine the reactions make sure the electrons lost must be equal to the electrons gained:

    CX4HX9OH+7 HX2O⟶4 COX2+24 eX−+24 HX+\ce{C4H9OH} + 7\ce{\,H2O} \longrightarrow \ce{4\,CO2} + \cancel{24 \ce{\,e-}} + \cancel{24 \ce{\,H+}}CX4​HX9​OH+7HX2​O⟶4COX2​+24eX−+24HX+

    6 OX2+24 eX−+24 HX+⟶12 HX2O\ce{\,O2} + \cancel{24 \ce{\,e-}} + \cancel{24 \ce{\,H+}} \longrightarrow \ce{12\,H2O}OX2​+24eX−+24HX+⟶12HX2​O

    CX4HX9OH+6 OX2⟶4 COX2+5 HX2O\ce{C4H9OH} + 6\ce{\,O2} \longrightarrow 4 \ce{\,CO2} + 5 \ce{\,H2O}CX4​HX9​OH+6OX2​⟶4COX2​+5HX2​O

    Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
    The shape of a titration curve reflects the chemical species present in solution at each stage. For a weak acid titrated with a strong base, the curve can be understood by examining four distinct regions:

    Region 1: Initial pH (0 cm3^33 NaOH added)
    Before any base is added, the solution contains only propanoic acid in water. As a weak acid, it partially dissociates according to its Ka:K_a:Ka​:

    CHX3CHX2COOH+HX2O⇌CHX3CHX2COOX−+HX3OX+\ce{CH3CH2COOH} + \ce{H2O} \rightleftharpoons \ce{CH3CH2COO-} + \ce{H3O+}CHX3​CHX2​COOH+HX2​O⇌CHX3​CHX2​COOX−+HX3​OX+

    The initial pH (2.76) is higher than it would be for a strong acid of the same concentration because only a small fraction of the acid molecules donate protons to water.

    Region 2: Buffer region (centered at 8.5  cm3\textit{\,cm}^3cm3)
    As NaOH is added, it neutralises propanoic acid to form propanoate ions:

    CHX3CHX2COOH+OHX−⟶CHX3CHX2COOX−+HX2O\ce{CH3CH2COOH} + \ce{OH-} \longrightarrow \ce{CH3CH2COO-} + \ce{H2O}CHX3​CHX2​COOH+OHX−⟶CHX3​CHX2​COOX−+HX2​O

    The solution now contains both the weak acid (HA) and its conjugate base (AX−),(\ce{A-}),(AX−), forming a buffer system. The pH in this region is governed by the Henderson−-−Hasselbalch equation:

    pH=pKa+log⁡[AX−][HA]\textrm{pH} = \textrm{p}K_a + \log\dfrac{[\ce{A-}]}{[\ce{HA}]}pH=pKa​+log[HA][AX−]​

    The curve rises gradually because the buffer resists pH change−-−added OHX−\ce{OH-}OHX− is consumed by HA rather than accumulating as free hydroxide ions.

    At the half−-−equivalence point (V=8.5 cm3),(V=8.5 \textrm{\,cm}^3),(V=8.5cm3), exactly half the acid has been neutralised, so [HA]=[AX−].[\ce{HA}]=[\ce{A-}].[HA]=[AX−]. The logarithmic term becomes zero, and pH=pKa=4.87.\textrm{pH} = \textrm{p}K_a = 4.87.pH=pKa​=4.87. This is why the curve passes through pH 4.87 at half the equivalence volume.

    Region 3: Equivalence point (17 cm3^33)
    At the equivalence point, all the propanoic acid has been converted to propanoate ions. The solution contains only the conjugate base, CHX3CHX2COOX−,\ce{CH3CH2COO^-},CHX3​CHX2​COOX−, which undergoes hydrolysis:

    CHX3CHX2COOX−+HX2O⇌CHX3CHX2COOH+OHX−\ce{CH3CH2COO−} + \ce{H2O} \rightleftharpoons \ce{CH3CH2COOH} + \ce{OH-}CHX3​CHX2​COOX−+HX2​O⇌CHX3​CHX2​COOH+OHX−

    This reaction produces hydroxide ions, making the solution basic (pH > 7). For this titration, the equivalence point pH is approximately 8.9.

    The curve is steep near the equivalence point because there is no longer a buffer system present. With virtually no weak acid remaining to neutralise added OHX−,\ce{OH-},OHX−, even a small excess of base causes a dramatic pH increase.

    Region 4: Post-equivalence (>17 cm3^33)
    Beyond the equivalence point, excess NaOH accumulates in solution. The pH is now controlled by the concentration of excess strong base and rises toward, but never reaches, the pH of the undiluted NaOH solution (pH 13.4). The curve levels off because each additional drop of base is diluted into an increasingly large total volume.

    Acid−-−base indicators change their colour according to the pH of the solution. Indicators exist in protonated and deprotonated forms, and the colour of these two is different. The transition from one species to the other occurs at pH=pKa\textrm{pH} = \textrm{p}K_apH=pKa​ of the indicator.

    HInColour A+HX2O⇌HX3OX++InX−Colour B\underset{\textrm{Colour A}}{\ce{HIn}} + \ce{H2O} \rightleftharpoons \ce{H3O+} + \underset{\textrm{Colour B}}{\ce{In-}}Colour AHIn​+HX2​O⇌HX3​OX++Colour BInX−​

    A suitable indicator must have a transition range that lies within the steep vertical region of the titration curve (approximately pH 8−-−10); therefore, phenolphthalein or phenol red could be used.

    add base: OHX−+CHX3CHX2COOH⟶HX2O+CHX3CHX2COOX− ✓\ce{OH-} + \ce{CH3CH2COOH} \longrightarrow \ce{H2O} + \ce{CH3CH2COO-} \: \checkmarkOHX−+CHX3​CHX2​COOH⟶HX2​O+CHX3​CHX2​COOX−✓

    Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
    The buffer consists of a weak acid and its conjugate base. In this case, the buffer region has a mixture of propanoic acid and propanoate ions. The buffer resists changes in the pH when a small amount of strong acid or base is added to it.

    If a strong acid is added to this buffer, it reacts with the propanoate ions, and the pH decreases only slightly because the strong acid is converted to a weak acid.

    HX++CHX3CHX2COOX−⟶CHX3CHX2COOH\ce{H+} + \ce{CH3CH2COO-} \longrightarrow \ce{CH3CH2COOH}HX++CHX3​CHX2​COOX−⟶CHX3​CHX2​COOH

    If a strong base is added to the buffer, it reacts with the propanoic acid to form its conjugate base (propanoate ion). Again, there is no significant impact on the resulting pH:

    OHX−+CHX3CHX2COOH⟶HX2O+CHX3CHX2COOX−\ce{OH-} + \ce{CH3CH2COOH} \longrightarrow \ce{H2O} + \ce{CH3CH2COO-}OHX−+CHX3​CHX2​COOH⟶HX2​O+CHX3​CHX2​COOX−

      The equilibrium constant expression for a general reaction

      a A(g)+b B(g)⇌c C(g)K=[C]c[A]a[B]ba \ce{\,A}\textrm{(g)} + b \ce{\,B}\textrm{(g)} \rightleftharpoons c \ce{\,C}\textrm{(g)} \hspace{2.em} K = \dfrac{{[\ce{C}]}^c}{{[\ce{A}]}^a{[\ce{B}]}^b}aA(g)+bB(g)⇌cC(g)K=[A]a[B]b[C]c​

      The equilibrium constant only includes gaseous and solution (aqueous) phase reactants and products. Since magnesium fluoride is a solid it does not appear in the equilibrium constant expression.

If the molar solubility of magnesium fluoride is x,x,x, [Mg2+]=x[\ce{Mg}^{2+}] = x[Mg2+]=x and [FX−]=2x.[\ce{F-}] = 2x.[FX−]=2x.. Substituting into the equilibrium consant expression,

      \mbox{}\\[-40pts]

      EffectReason
      Adding sodium fluoride \newline to the saturated solutionshifts left, \newline more solid formsmore product added✓\checkmark✓
      Increasing the temperatureshifts left, \newline more solid formsproceeds in endothermic direction✓\checkmark✓
      Using a catalystno effectforward and reverse rates increased equally, \newline same equilibrium position✓\checkmark✓

       \  

      Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
      Adding sodium fluoride: NaF is a soluble salt that fully dissociates, increasing the fluoride ion concentration. According to Le Chaˆ\textrm{\^{a}}aˆtelier's principle, the system shifts to oppose this increase in [FX−][\ce{F-}][FX−] by shifting left. This reduces the solubility of magnesium fluoride, more MgFX2\ce{MgF2}MgFX2​ will precipitate.

      Increasing temperature: The dissolution is exothermic (ΔH<0)(\Delta H < 0)(ΔH<0), meaning heat is released as MgFX2\ce{MgF2}MgFX2​ dissolves. When the temperature of a system at equilibrium is increased, it shifts in the endothermic direction. For magnesium fluoride, the solubility will decrease and more will precipitate.

      Using a catalyst: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, but it affects the forward and reverse reactions equally. Therefore, equilibrium is reached faster, but the position of the equilibrium is unchanged.

      no AND mechanisms can only be disproved ✓\checkmark✓

      Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
      Confirmation of the experimentally determined rate expression shows that the proposed mechanism is consistent with the kinetic data, but it does not prove that the mechanism is correct. Different sequences of elementary steps can produce the same overall rate law and overall equation. Kinetic evidence can therefore eliminate mechanisms that are incompatible with the rate expression, but it cannot uniquely establish a single correct pathway without additional experimental evidence.

    4.  \   \mbox{}\\[-25pts]

    \hspace{1.2em}✓✓\checkmark \checkmark✓✓

    Award M1 for products lower in energy than reactants.
    Award M2 for two maxima where Step 1 has a lower activation energy than Step 2.

    Further Explanation:‾\textrm{\underline{Further Explanation:}}Further Explanation:​
    The proposed mechanism has two elementary steps, so the potential energy diagram must show two transition states and therefore two peaks. Between the two peaks there is a local minimum representing the intermediate NX2OX2,\ce{N2O2},NX2​OX2​, which is produced in Step 1 and consumed in Step 2.

    Because Step 1 is described as a fast equilibrium, its activation energy must be smaller than that of Step 2. Therefore, the first peak must be lower than the second peak. Step 2 is the rate−-−determining step, so its activation energy is the largest barrier on the diagram. This is why the second peak must be the highest point on the curve.

    The reaction is exothermic so the products are more stable than the reactants. The final energy level must lie below the initial reactant energy level.

    Award M1 for maximum lower and to the right, start at origin, always above x−x-x−axis.
    Award M2 for adding EaE_aEa​ and shading the molecules with enough energy to react.

    When the temperature is increased from T1T_1T1​ to T2,T_2,T2​, the Maxwell−-−Boltzmann distribution becomes broader and lower in height, and the peak shifts toward higher kinetic energy. The activation energy EaE_aEa​ does not change, but the area under the curve to the right of EaE_aEa​ increases at the higher temperature (see the shaded region on the graph).

    This means that at T2T_2T2​ a greater proportion of molecules have kinetic energy greater than or equal to the activation energy. Therefore, a greater fraction of collisions are successful, so the rate of reaction increases.

All the questions you could need! Sorted by topic and arranged by difficulty, with mark schemes and video solutions for every question.

Paper 1B

New

Flashcards

Use multiple-choice questions and study crucial terminology on desktop or mobile app to improve your marks!

Resources designed around the most important concepts, techniques, and skills required for success in the Chemistry IA.

Summary Notes
